food.text: By 1800 Japan was producing more sugar than it was importing. Okinawa and Amami Ōshima specialized in brown sugar, while the island of Shikoku made a fine-grained sugar known as wasanbon, which the elite favored for making wagashi.

Sugar consumption grew across the 19th century as workers in Japan developed the habit of tea breaks. This created demand for snacks that could be served alongside tea, and advertisements showed children and adults eating sugar, often with sweet peddlers crying out their promotions.

British traders introduced curry powder to Meiji-era Japan, where it was used to make Japanese curry, known as karē. It is usually eaten as karē raisu, with rice and often pickled vegetables on the same plate, and is more a thick stew than a curry.

Hotteok, a filled pancake, originated in Qing dynasty China and was first brought into Joseon Korea during the 19th century. Its dough is made from wheat flour, water, milk, sugar and yeast, and it is filled with a sweet mixture.

Japanese Chinese cuisine, called chūka ryōri, is a fusion of Japanese and Chinese traditions that has evolved since the late 19th century. Most of its dishes have roots in Cantonese cuisine, and ramen primarily derives from Cantonese noodle soups.

Japan annexed Taiwan in 1895 and began developing a sugar industry there, which started operations in late 1900. By 1903 almost all of Japan's sugar came from Taiwan, and average annual consumption had risen to an estimated 12 pounds (5.4 kg) per person from 5 pounds in 1888.

Curry's spread across Japan is attributed to its use in the Japanese Army and Navy, which adopted it extensively as convenient field and naval canteen cooking. This let even conscripts from the remotest countryside experience the dish.

It is generally believed that Chinese merchants who immigrated to and settled in Korea around the late 19th century made and sold hotteok at cheap prices, which helped spread the dish throughout Korea. It is said that Chinese merchants who entered Korea during the Imo Incident did not return to their homeland even after their country was destroyed. They opened restaurants and sold food to make a living, and hotteok was one of the foods they sold.

Until the late 19th century, Korean transportation networks were not well developed, so each provincial region preserved its own characteristic tastes and cooking methods. Local specialty foods reflected the climate, the agriculture and the natural foods available in each area.

Furai, breaded seafood or vegetables, developed in the late 19th and early 20th century as a form of yōshoku, or Western-influenced Japanese cuisine. The word is a transliteration of the English word fry, and the main types are ebi furai (shrimp), kaki furai (oyster) and aji furai (horse mackerel).
Japan consumed less sugar than Western countries in the 19th century and regarded Western sweets with distaste. The smell of milk and butter was considered off-putting.

art.text: During the Meiji Period (1868–1912), Japanese art saw an abrupt influx of Western styles. The country absorbed and imitated foreign culture, and Japanese art in turn considerably influenced 19th-century Western painting.

After the Meiji Restoration, Japan underwent intense Westernization, and the government invited foreign architects to work in Japan and teach new Japanese architects. The British architect Josiah Conder trained many prominent Meiji era architects, including Kingo Tatsuno, Tatsuzō Sone and Tokuma Katayama.

For the 1876 Centennial International Exhibition in Philadelphia, the Japanese government created a Centennial Office. It sent a special envoy to secure space for the 30,000 items that would be displayed.

In 1890 the Teishitsu Gigeiin system, Artist to the Imperial Household, was created to recognise distinguished artists. Seventy were appointed from 1890 to 1944, including the painter and lacquer artist Shibata Zeshin and the cloisonné enamel artist Namikawa Yasuyuki.

Japanese-Western Eclectic Architecture deliberately combined Japanese and Western components in one building. The style emerged in Yokohama in the Bakumatsu period of 1853 to 1867 and spread throughout Japan after the 1868 Meiji Restoration.

The Japan Art Academy was founded in 1907 as the Fine Arts Reviewing Committee of the Ministry of Education, to provide quality standards and a venue for exhibitions in late Meiji Japan. Its first annual exhibition, called the Bunten, was held that same year.

The Japanese government created a semi-public company, the Kiritsu Kosho Kaisha, to promote and commercialize exports of art. It also established the Hakurankai Jimukyoku, or Exhibition Bureau, to maintain quality standards.
Kingo Tatsuno's early works had a Venetian style influenced by John Ruskin. His later works, such as the Bank of Japan (1896) and Tōkyō Station (1914), have a more Beaux-Arts feel.
Tokuma Katayama was more influenced by the French Second Empire style. It can be seen in his Nara National Museum, built in 1894, and the Kyōto National Museum, built in 1895.

Early examples of Japanese-Western Eclectic Architecture include the First National Bank of Japan, built by the Mistui Group in 1872. The Kaichi School Museum building followed in 1876, and Seika Restaurant in 1881.

The Japan Art Association was renamed in 1887 with Prince Arisugawa Taruhito as president, under a policy of preserving pure traditional paintings. Its membership grew from 478 in 1888 to a peak of 1,560 in December 1903.

war.text: The Russo-Japanese War was fought between 1904 and 1905 over rival imperial ambitions in Manchuria and the Korean Empire. Major land battles took place on the Liaodong Peninsula and near Mukden, while naval battles were fought in the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan.

The First Sino-Japanese War, fought between the Qing dynasty and Japan, was primarily a struggle for influence over Korea. After about seven months of Japanese gains on land and sea, including the loss of Port Arthur and Weihaiwei, the Qing sued for peace in February 1895.

The Bakufu modernized its army through the assistance of French military missions, including the one associated with Jules Brunet. Even after France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871), it was still considered an example in the military field and a model for the Imperial Japanese Army.

Japan opened the Russo-Japanese War with a surprise attack on the Russian Pacific Fleet at Port Arthur on 9 February 1904. Japanese troops then landed in Korea and crossed the Yalu River into Manchuria in May.

In 1894 Japan sent an expeditionary force of 8,000 troops that landed at Incheon after the Qing sent troops to help suppress the Tonghak Peasant Revolution. The army moved to Seoul, seized the Korean emperor, and set up a pro-Japanese government on 23 July 1894.

Japan's modernized army defeated the Satsuma rebellion, led by Saigō Takamori, in 1877. A French military mission invited in 1872 had set out to organize the army and establish a military educational system, and founded the Ichigaya Military Academy in 1874.

In 1811 Hong Gyeong-rae led the first significant peasant uprising of massive scale in Korea. A large famine had swept the province, and by September 1811 Hong had gathered an army on the island of Chudo. The rebels later capitulated after a 4-month siege, when government forces collapsed the walls of Jeongju Fortress with eleven tons of explosives dug under the wall. All male rebels above the age of ten were executed.

In 1872 Japan invited a second French military mission, which worked until 1880 to organize the army and set up a military educational system. It established the Ichigaya Military Academy, built in 1874. In 1877 the modernized Imperial Japanese Army defeated the Satsuma rebellion led by Saigō Takamori.

The Russian Baltic Fleet sailed for seven months and 18,000 nautical miles from the Baltic Sea to reinforce the Pacific Fleet, reaching the Sea of Japan in May 1905. The Japanese Combined Fleet intercepted it at the Battle of Tsushima on 27-28 May 1905 and virtually annihilated it. The Russians lost eight battleships, numerous smaller vessels and more than 5,000 men, against Japanese losses of three torpedo boats and 116 men. Only three Russian vessels escaped to Vladivostok.

Japanese forces laid siege to Port Arthur in August 1904. Their frontal assaults on the fortified hilltops were defeated with Japanese casualties in the thousands, and several large underground mines were exploded in late December before the city fell in January 1905. In March 1905 they took Mukden, the Manchurian capital, after days of harsh fighting in which the Russians suffered an estimated 90,000 casualties and the Japanese also took heavy casualties. Theodore Roosevelt mediated the Treaty of Portsmouth that ended the war.

On 25 July 1894 the Japanese Navy won the Battle of Pungdo and sank the steamer Kowshing, which was carrying 1,200 Qing reinforcements. The Qing troops remaining in Korea could be supplied only by sea. A declaration of war followed on 1 August.

A policy of persecuting Catholics under the regent Heungseon Daewongun led directly to the unsuccessful French Campaign against Korea in 1866. The regent was the main proponent of isolationism during the mid-1860s.

France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War did not stop it from being seen as a military model for Japan. The Bakufu had earlier modernized its army with help from French military missions, including Jules Brunet.

literature.text: Natsume Sōseki, Mori Ōgai and Shiga Naoya were instrumental in adopting and adapting Western literary conventions and techniques. Shiga Naoya was called the "god of the novel" as the most prominent "I novel" writer.

Kyokutei Bakin took twenty-eight years, from 1814 to 1842, to complete his extremely popular fantasy and historical romance Nansō Satomi Hakkenden. It was one of the yomihon, a genre whose range included horror, crime stories, morality stories, comedy and pornography, often accompanied by colorful woodcut prints.

The Go Gawa poetry club was a famous poetry club in Edo in the early 19th century. Its artists often wrote poetry on illustrated surimono and signed their work with a symbol resembling an hourglass, shaped like the number five. By 1836 the club had already met 1,600 times.

Romanticism was brought into Japanese literature by Mori Ōgai with his anthology of translated poems in 1889. Tōson Shimazaki carried it to its height, alongside magazines such as Myōjō and Bungaku-kai in the early 1900s.

The Go Gawa club was led by Rokujuen, a kabuki actor who was also a scholar of Japanese classics and a translator of Chinese fables. He had been banished from Edo after a confrontation with authorities over his management of an inn, and he returned at the beginning of the Bunka era in 1804.
Mori Ōgai wrote modern novels including The Dancing Girl in 1890 and The Wild Geese in 1911. He later turned to writing historical novels.

Natsume Sōseki followed the satire of I Am a Cat with Botchan in 1906 and Sanshirō in 1908, which depicted fresh and pure youth. In his later works, including Kokoro in 1914, he pursued transcendence of human emotions and egoism. His last novel, Light and Darkness, was left unfinished in 1916.

The first major surimono and kyōka anthology of the Go Gawa club, Shunkyōjō, appeared in 1810 and resembled actors' critiques known as hyōbanki. In 1811 the club published another major anthology, kyōka hyōbanki, as a critique of other kyōka poets.

Kyōchōshi Fumimaro, a disciple of Rokujuen, kept publishing major anthologies for the Go Gawa club, including Haro no uta and Hajime no haro no kyōka-shū in 1816-17. Both anthologies were themed around spring.

science.text: During the Meiji period (1868–1912), the Empire of Japan pursued rapid industrialization and modernization. It emerged as the most developed state in Asia and as an industrialized world power.

Silk helped pay for Japan's modernization. France absorbed more than 50% of Japan's raw silk production between 1865 and 1885, and the silk exports allowed Japan to gather currencies to purchase foreign goods and technologies.

The popular idea that Korea's turtle ships were ironclads may come from the 19th century. Historian Samuel Hawley suggests it began with the writings of late 19th-century Westerners returning from Korea, starting no earlier than about 1880, when Western-type ironclad warships were rising to global prominence.

Japan relied on France for several aspects of its modernization. French help was important in developing a shipbuilding industry during the early years of the Imperial Japanese Navy, with Emile Bertin named in connection with this work. France also helped Japan develop a legal code.

Jules Verne's novels were the first influential science fiction translated into Japanese. Around the World in Eighty Days, part of whose plot is set in Japan, was published in 1878–1880 and was followed by his other works with immense popularity. The word kagaku shōsetsu, meaning "scientific novel", was coined as early as 1886.
tags: Around the World in Eighty Days

science.text: By 1875, Lyon had become the world center for silk processing, and Yokohama had become the center for supplying the raw material. By 1910 Japan had become the first world producer of silk, though the United States had overtaken France as the first importer of Japanese silk from around 1885.

During the General Sherman incident, the Koreans built an improvised turtle ship protected by metal sheeting and cowhides to destroy the General Sherman. It failed to penetrate the American ship's iron hull, and one Korean sailor was killed in the attempt.

Shunrō Oshikawa is generally considered the ancestor of Japanese science fiction. His debut work Kaitei Gunkan (Undersea warship), published in 1900, described submarines and predicted a coming Russo-Japanese War.
When the French Navy threatened Korea, the government ordered an ironclad ship built "like the turtle ship." Despite all efforts, the design failed to float.

politics.text: On 27 February 1876, Japan imposed the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1876 on Korea, forcing it open to Japanese trade. The act blocked any other power from dominating Korea and aimed to end the centuries-old Chinese suzerainty.

In 1905 Korea became a protectorate of Japan after the Russo-Japanese War. Prince Itō served as the first Resident-General of Korea, but he was assassinated in 1909 by the independence activist An Jung-geun at the train station in Harbin, China. Japan annexed Korea the following year.

In January 1876, Japan used gunboat diplomacy to pressure Joseon Korea into signing an unequal treaty. It granted extraterritorial rights to Japanese citizens and opened three Korean ports to Japanese trade, similar to the rights western powers gained in Japan after Commodore Perry's visit.

On 22 August 1910, Japan effectively annexed Korea with a treaty signed by Ye Wanyong, Prime Minister of Korea, and Terauchi Masatake. Terauchi, who had been Japan's Minister of War, became the first Governor-General of Chōsen.

In 1897, King Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire and took the title of Emperor to assert Korea's independence. His court also sought foreign powers for military technology, especially Russia, to fend off the Japanese.

Japan ceded southern Sakhalin to Russia in 1875 in exchange for the Kuril Islands under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg. After winning the Russo-Japanese War, Japan received southern Sakhalin under the Treaty of Portsmouth and in 1907 established a colonial government, renaming it Karafuto Prefecture.

Two months after Japan defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War, Korea lost its diplomatic sovereignty in the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905, signed by the Five Eulsa Traitors. Gojong refused to sign it and tried to bring the treaty to the attention of the international community and convince leading powers it was illegitimate, but to no avail. Yi Han-eung, whom Gojong had sent to London in 1901 as acting diplomatic minister, killed himself in protest in May 1905, and Gojong's letter to Theodore Roosevelt, delivered by Homer Hulbert, arrived after the treaty was already signed.

On 8 October 1895, the Japanese convinced officers of the Hullyeondae that the royal family was seeking help from the Russians, and plotted to assassinate Queen Min. One thousand Hullyeondae troops stormed the palace and defeated the Capital Guards, which let the ronin kill her.

In 1882 Korea signed a treaty with China that reduced it to a semi-colonial tributary state, with King Gojong unable to appoint diplomats without Chinese approval. Li Hongzhang set China's policy toward Joseon, and Yuan Shikai implemented it as resident official from 1885 to 1894.

In 1885, China and Japan signed a treaty agreeing to withdraw their troops from Korea. Neither country would send forces there without notifying the other in advance. It followed a 1884 attempt by pro-Japanese reformers to overthrow Korea's conservative government; China intervened to suppress the rebellion, leading to a clash in which several Japanese guards were killed.
After Queen Min's death, Gojong ordered the deaths of pro-Japanese officials, which ended the Gabo Reform. He also disbanded the Military Training Division for its part in the assassination.

philosophy.text: In 1860, Choe Je-u, a member of an impoverished yangban family, founded the Donghak ("Eastern Learning") movement. He meant it as a counter-force to the rise of "foreign religions", which in his view included Buddhism and Christianity. He saw them as part of Seohak, the wave of Western influence.

From the late Meiji to Taishō period, the Kyoto School tried to harmonize Western thought with Eastern thought such as Zen Buddhism. Nishida Kitaro fused Zen and Western thought. He insisted on pure experience, in which there is no opposition between subjectivity and objectivity.

Donghak arose in 1860 as an alternative to Catholicism, called "Western Learning", which was gaining momentum among Korea's lower classes. It taught that the divine could be lived out on earth, so local landlords and foreign powers viewed it unfavorably. They oversaw Choe Je-u's trial and execution in 1864.

The Joseon kingdom adopted an especially strict version of Neo-Confucianism and suppressed and marginalised Korean Buddhism. Buddhist monasteries were destroyed, and their number dropped from several hundreds to a mere thirty-six. Buddhism was eradicated from the life of towns as monks and nuns were prohibited from entering them and were marginalised to the mountains, and these restrictions lasted until the 19th century.

Catholicism was secretly spread in Korea by missionaries despite a prohibition, leading to multiple persecutions by the court in the 19th century. Some actions ran counter to Confucian ideology. The Hwang Sa-Yeong White Book incident, sparked by Catholics seeking freedom of religious belief, worsened the Sinyu Persecution in 1801.

In the 1860s, Japan experienced great social turmoil and rapid modernization, and new religious movements appeared. Tenrikyo, Kurozumikyo and Oomoto were directly influenced by Shinto and shamanism. They are sometimes called Japan's three large new religions, or "old new religions".

Socialist thought spread in Japan as capitalism grew, but the security police law of 1900 suppressed social movements, and in the High Treason Incident of 1910 socialists were pressed down by the military and the fascist government. Kōtoku Shūsui first tried to realize socialism through the Diet, then became a unionist and argued for direct action by a general strike. He was executed as the mastermind of the High Treason Incident of 1910.

Followers of Donghak were severely persecuted until the Protectorate Treaty of 1905, which guaranteed freedom of religion. On 1 December 1905, Son Byong-hi officially renamed Donghak as Cheondoism, "religion of the Celestial Way", to modernize it and legitimize it in the eyes of the Japanese, who had strong influence over Korea at the time. A constitution and a Central General Bureau were then laid out.

Kawakami Hajime wrote newspaper articles about poverty. At first he emphasized personal remodeling to solve it, but he later became a Marxist. He then argued for social remodeling by social compulsion.

Cheondoism venerates Cheon ("Sky" or "Heaven") as the ultimate principle of good and justice, called by the honorific Haneullim. According to church doctrine, humans and things are not created by a supernatural God but generated by a God-nature present in all living and unliving things.

In 1909, Kotaro Yamaoka converted to Islam in Bombay after contacting Abdurreshid Ibrahim, and took the name Omar Yamaoka. He became the first Japanese to go on the Hajj. He traveled seeking the Ottoman Sultan and Caliph's approval for a mosque in Tokyo, which was granted in 1910.

culture.text: Baseball reached Japan through the treaty ports, opened in 1859, where American and British expatriates played it alongside cricket. In 1872 an American, Horace Wilson, introduced it as a school sport while teaching English at the Kaisei Academy in Tokyo.

Japan was forced to open to the West after 1853, and by the late 1850s it had become a major tea exporter. It sold mainly to the United States, where Japanese sencha was a great success, although teas meant for foreign markets were often of poor quality.

In 1873, after the Meiji Restoration, Japan rescinded its ban on Christianity and promulgated freedom of religion. Protestant missionaries then began to proselytise in Japan, though they were never as successful there as in Korea.

The Kami and Buddhas Separation Act of 1868 formally separated Buddhism from Shinto, and Buddhist temples from Shinto shrines. This broke an association that had lasted well over a thousand years and radically changed the history of Japanese architecture.

In 1896 a team from Tokyo's Ichikō high school convincingly beat resident foreigners from the Yokohama Country & Athletic Club in a match at Yokohama. The Japanese press praised the students as national heroes, and news of the win greatly boosted baseball's popularity as a school sport.

Japan's tea trade grew sophisticated by the early 19th century, and around 1835 gyokuro emerged as one of the most famous teas. The national tea trade was controlled by guilds of merchants and wholesalers who held a monopoly on the product.

The Japanese new religions Tenrikyo, Kurozumikyo and Oomoto arose amid the social turmoil of the Bakumatsu period in the 1860s. Sometimes called Japan's three large new religions, they were directly influenced by Shinto and shamanism.

During the Meiji period, the traditional syncretism between Shinto and Buddhism ended and Shinto became the national religion. Buddhist monks lost the government protection they had enjoyed for centuries and faced radical difficulties in sustaining their institutions.

Choe Je-u, a member of an impoverished yangban family, founded the Donghak ("Eastern Learning") movement in 1860 as a counter-force to the rise of "foreign religions", and it became the basis of Cheondoism. The movement became so influential among common people that in 1864 the Joseon government sentenced Choe Je-u to death, and he was executed.

Tsuneo Matsudaira told the Japan Society of the UK in London in 1907 that after the Ichikō victory, baseball spread "like a fire in a dry field" across the country. Some months later, even primary school children far from Tōkyō were playing with bats and balls.
The first organized adult baseball team in Japan, the Shimbashi Athletic Club, was established in 1878. This came six years after baseball was introduced as a school sport.

Protestantism became engrained in Korea in the 1890s, along with a network of schools and hospitals. Protestant missionaries labeled shamans and indigenous religious practices "devil worship" and led campaigns to burn idols, ancestral tablets, shamans' tools and clothes, and shrines. According to missionary reports, these were "destroyed as were the "books" (magic scrolls) in Ephesus". In 1896 the police began to arrest shamans, destroy shrines and burn ritual tools, and the newspaper The Independent acclaimed these events.
